guess.doing: Write your best guess before you see anything.
guess.why: A guess you committed to, even a wrong one, makes the real answer stick harder when it arrives.
guess.source: Richland, Kornell & Kao 2009, wrong guesses boost later learning

anchor.doing: Use one true fact to predict what happens next.
anchor.why: A real fact gives you something solid to reason from, and a prediction shows you where your picture is thin.
anchor.source: Onionskin research brief, section 9: start concrete, then abstract

contrast.doing: Compare two look-alike cases and write why they differ.
contrast.why: Lining up two cases makes your mind match what each part does, so the shared structure shows up on its own.
contrast.source: Gentner, Loewenstein & Thompson 2003, comparing cases beats studying separately

stress.doing: Test your fix on three extreme cases and watch what breaks.
stress.why: Extreme cases expose rules that only work in easy cases, so a break shows exactly which part of your model is wrong.
stress.source: Clement 2009, experts test models with extreme cases

draw.doing: Sketch the model from memory, then write its rule.
draw.why: Drawing makes you pick the parts, link them, and put them together, and a wrong picture shows a wrong idea.
draw.source: Wammes, Meade & Fernandes 2016, drawing roughly doubles recall

neighbor.doing: Pick which idea this is, against its look-alike cousin.
neighbor.why: Telling similar ideas apart is a skill of its own, and practicing the choice teaches you when each one applies.
neighbor.source: Brunmair & Richter 2019, mixing look-alikes sharpens discrimination

transfer.doing: Say the same idea in a totally different field.
transfer.why: Ideas rarely carry over to new settings on their own, so you build the bridge by naming where else it applies.
transfer.source: Barnett & Ceci 2002, far transfer must be designed for

done.doing: Read the mistake card, then save it to your Notebook.
done.why: Seeing why a wrong idea felt right lets you replace the idea itself, not just patch one answer.
done.source: Chi 2005, stubborn misconceptions need a new category
